g.data-help:
What is this and how to use.. This is a diagram made to better understand and get an overview of kubernetes security.
It's not complete (but you are welcome to submitt a PR/issue), nor is it perfect, it is biased and it might not be for you.
It might however help you to discuss kubernetes in a security-context with your team, or just to get a better understanding yourself.
The drawing is most likely an overkill. It is not ment as a "solution" or design. It's also quite busy, with a ton of elements. It's not ment to "explain" everything, but something you can sit down with and browse around and maybe learn something new.
Also, it is on-prem... For non on-prem, it might not be that relevant.

g.data-help:
What is an "operator"
Operators in Kubernetes extend the control plane by automating the management of complex applications or infrastructure using custom resources and controllers.
For example, a system operator can create defaults like Namespaces, or manage external resources through custom objects like a "Tofu" resource controlling infrastructure outside the cluster.
Kubernetes can serve as a generic orchestration engine—beyond just container workloads.

Secret Watch / Read
The Gateway controller watches and reads the certificate Secret to build and update dataplane TLS configuration.

g.data-help:
TLS Certificate Usage
The gateway proxy uses the certificate material for TLS termination. How it receives the certificate (mounted Secret vs dynamic delivery) depends on the implementation.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 8px; height: 1px; padding-top: 310px; margin-left: 1419px;

g.data-help:
ResourceQuota vs LimitRange
ResourceQuota limits the total resources and object counts a namespace can use, which helps prevent one team/app from exhausting shared cluster capacity (for example creating too many pods/services or consuming too much CPU, memory, or storage).
LimitRange sets default and min/max resource requests and limits for pods/containers in that namespace, which helps prevent unsafe or unstable workloads (for example containers with no memory limit, or requests/limits that are far too high or too low).

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 16px; height: 1px; padding-top: 1158px; margin-left: 1518px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
The Container Process
Containerized workloads are secured through PodSecurityContext/SecurityContext, Pod Security Standards (PSA), namespace isolation, and runtime enforcement. Tools like Falco (eBPF) monitor behavior, while KubeArmor enforces policies. Enterprise options include Sysdig Secure, Tetragon, Prisma Cloud, and the open-source NeuVector.
Syscalls are restricted by default; escapes often rely on misconfigurations such as excessive Linux capabilities, unfiltered syscalls, insecure mounts, or relaxed namespace settings.
Linux namespaces isolate PIDs, networking, and other kernel features; cgroups control CPU/memory and can freeze containers for forensics.
Runtime policies like runAsNonRoot or fixed UID/GID can be set at the container/pod level or baked into the image.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 122, 122), rgb(198, 84, 84)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(122, 20, 20), rgb(255, 183, 183));

g.data-help:
Network Control
Network policies can enforce L3/L4 restrictions using eBPF or iptables, while L7 policies are enforced via proxies (e.g., Envoy).
Some CNIs support admin-level policies that cannot be overridden by namespace users, enabling enforcement of cluster-wide or organizational security standards.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 122, 122), rgb(198, 84, 84)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(122, 20, 20), rgb(255, 183, 183));

g.data-tags: level-2 pri-1 Network Network.Ingress Ingress Ingress.Controller
g.data-help:
Ingress
Kubernetes Ingress resources configure an ingress controller (e.g., NGINX, HAProxy) to handle inbound traffic. Controllers support annotations for TLS settings, authentication, WAF (e.g., ModSecurity), and other security features.
Routing is typically based on SNI (FQDN) and HTTP-layer data such as path, method, or headers. Secure configuration of the ingress controller is critical, including rate limiting, header validation, and TLS hardening.
For new designs, prefer Gateway API where possible. Gateway API provides a more structured and extensible model for routing, policy attachment, and role separation, and is the main direction of ongoing ecosystem development.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 122, 122), rgb(198, 84, 84)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(122, 20, 20), rgb(255, 183, 183));

g.data-help: Kubernetes API The Kubernetes API is the primary control plane entry point and must be tightly secured. All access passes through two stages: authentication and authorization. API call is first ratelimited using priority and fairness. Authentication verifies the caller (client certificates, bearer tokens, OIDC, or webhook tokens). Anonymous requests are allowed by default (should be disabled in production). Authorization decides if the authenticated identity may act. Kubernetes supports: - RBAC (Role-Based Access Control): recommended and widely adopted. - Webhook Authorization: delegate decisions to an external policy engine. - ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control): legacy and strongly discouraged; keep only for backward compatibility and plan to migrate off it. RBAC grants fine-grained verbs (GET, CREATE, etc.) over resources and API groups via roles/bindings. ABAC uses JSON policy files but is harder to audit and operate at scale. Enable API server audit logging and ship logs to a remote backend for monitoring and incident response.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 122, 122), rgb(198, 84, 84)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(122, 20, 20), rgb(255, 183, 183));

g.data-help: RBAC RBAC authorizes a request by matching the caller (User/Group/ServiceAccount) to bindings, which reference roles containing rules (verbs/resources/apiGroups). Role and RoleBindings * Role: used by RoleBinding (same namespace) * ClusterRole (cluster-scoped): used by ClusterRoleBinding (cluster-wide) or RoleBinding (namespaced) * RoleBinding (namespaced) can reference Role or ClusterRole * ClusterRoleBinding (cluster-scoped) can reference only ClusterRole Subjects * User (global): not a Kubernetes resource; comes from authentication (cert/OIDC/webhook) * Group (global): not a resource; assigned by the identity provider * ServiceAccount (namespaced resource): must include namespace in bindings (also in ClusterRoleBinding). RoleBindings can only use ServiceAccounts from their own namespace Rules specify apiGroups, resources, resourceNames (optional), and verbs (e.g., get,list,watch,create,update,patch,delete). Non-resource URLs use nonResourceURLs. Warnings * Wildcards: avoid "*" for verbs/resources/apiGroups unless truly needed * escalate verb (on roles/clusterroles): allows creating/updating roles with permissions beyond your own * bind verb (on clusterroles): allows binding clusterroles you don't otherwise “own” * impersonate verb: restrict tightly; lets callers act as other users/groups/SAs (Impersonation docs) * Node/proxy (e.g. nodes/proxy, nodes/*, services/proxy, pods/proxy): Permissions that enable proxying via the API server can look harmless for monitoring, but effectively grant access to node/kubelet (and other proxied) HTTP endpoints. Treat as high-risk: avoid wildcards, scope tightly (resourceNames/namespaces), and only grant if you fully understand the blast radius and the exact endpoints the client can reach. This includes the GET verb!

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 122, 122), rgb(198, 84, 84)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(122, 20, 20), rgb(255, 183, 183));

g.data-help:
Namespaces
Namespaces are logical boundaries used to apply security controls such as network policies, RBAC, and runtime restrictions.
While not a security mechanism by themselves, they enable isolation between workloads and enforce separation of concerns.
Many controls are applied per namespace, including Pod Security Admission (PSA) profiles, ResourceQuota, LimitRange, NetworkPolicy, and the default ServiceAccount used by pods unless explicitly overridden.
This makes namespaces important for multi-tenancy, workload isolation, and applying different security baselines across teams or environments.
Do not confuse Kubernetes namespaces with Linux process namespaces inside containers.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 122, 122), rgb(198, 84, 84)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(122, 20, 20), rgb(255, 183, 183));

g.data-help:
Image Repository
Container images should be scanned for vulnerabilities before being stored in or pulled from the image repository.
Use tools that enforce image admission policies, signature verification, and vulnerability thresholds to block untrusted or outdated images.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 122, 122), rgb(198, 84, 84)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(122, 20, 20), rgb(255, 183, 183));

g.data-help:
Gateway
Kubernetes Gateway resources are part of Gateway API and define how traffic enters the cluster, including listeners (ports, protocols, hostnames) and TLS configuration (for example certificate references).
A Gateway is attached to a GatewayClass (implementation/controller) and is typically used together with Route resources (such as HTTPRoute or TCPRoute) that define traffic matching and forwarding behavior.
From a security perspective, Gateway is a key enforcement point for exposed services: it defines which protocols and hostnames are accepted, where TLS is terminated, and which certificates are used. Additional security controls are typically attached through policy resources (for example authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and WAF-related controls), while routes define how traffic is forwarded.
Gateway API separates infrastructure ownership (GatewayClass / Gateway) from application routing (*Route) and policy attachment (*Policy), making it a more structured and extensible model for secure, modern traffic management.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 122, 122), rgb(198, 84, 84)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(122, 20, 20), rgb(255, 183, 183));

g.data-help:
GatewayClass
GatewayClass selects which Gateway API controller implementation manages a Gateway (for example Envoy Gateway, Kong, Traefik, NGINX Gateway Fabric, or a cloud-managed implementation).
This is a key trust boundary: controllers differ in supported spec versions, conformance level, feature maturity, and security/policy behavior. Gateway API conformance helps validate what is actually implemented.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 122, 122), rgb(198, 84, 84)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(122, 20, 20), rgb(255, 183, 183));

g.data-help:
Pod Security Admission (PSA)
Pod Security Admission (PSA) enforces a baseline security level for pods in a namespace by validating pod specs at admission time (before the pod is created).
It uses namespace labels to apply standard Pod Security profiles (privileged, baseline, restricted) and can block insecure settings such as privileged containers, excessive Linux capabilities, unsafe host access, or other risky pod configurations.
PSA is an important preventive control for reducing attack surface and stopping insecure workloads before they are deployed.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 122, 122), rgb(198, 84, 84)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(122, 20, 20), rgb(255, 183, 183));

g.data-help:
Service Portal
Non-admin users should request cluster resources through a service portal instead of direct kubectl access. This portal can generate GitOps-compatible manifests and apply policy-based validation before committing to Git.
It must be separate from administrative tools and enforce access control and input validation.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Container image
Container runtimes can be configured to only allow signed images using tools like sigstore/cosign. Admission controllers such as Kyverno can enforce signature verification and additional build metadata (e.g., SLSA provenance).
Images should also be scanned for vulnerabilities before deployment and flagged or blocked based on severity thresholds.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Mounted volumes and env-vars
External data is often injected into pods via environment variables or projected volumes. These are typically read-only and can include ConfigMaps, Secrets, or dynamic runtime values like the pod IP or namespace.
When a pod needs to interact with the Kubernetes API, a service account token is automatically mounted as a projected volume. Ensure proper RBAC scoping for the associated service account to avoid privilege escalation.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Internal pod egress
Egress traffic from a pod to other services inside the cluster can be controlled using NetworkPolicies, similar to ingress rules. However, egress rules are often overlooked, as ingress is more commonly enforced.
Define explicit egress policies to restrict which services a pod can communicate with, reducing lateral movement and attack surface in case of compromise.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Secrets and ConfigMaps
Secrets and ConfigMaps can be encrypted at rest using encryption providers configured on the API server. The decryption keys are typically stored inside the cluster, often on disk.
For improved security, use external KMS providers (e.g., HashiCorp Vault, AWS KMS) to manage keys and prevent key compromise within the cluster.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
system:masters group
The 'system:masters' group is a built-in Kubernetes group that bypasses the authorization layer and grants full administrative access to the cluster.
It should only be used for initial bootstrapping or controlled RBAC testing. Ensure no regular users or service accounts are members of this group. Monitor and audit usage carefully—this group should be empty in production environments.
g.data-tags: level-3 pri-2 Api Api.Authn Api.Authz Api.Admission

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Operators and Infrastructure Workloads
Operators act on custom Kubernetes resources (e.g., Certificates) via standard controllers. They typically run as Deployments and require RBAC access to specific APIs.
Treat operators like any other workload: apply strict access controls, run them on dedicated nodes if needed, and isolate privileges based on least privilege principles.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Kubernetes Distributions and OS Choices
Choose a Kubernetes distribution and OS designed for security and minimal attack surface. Avoid general-purpose OSes that require separate patching.
Consider immutable, minimal, and hardened distros (e.g., Talos, Flatcar, Bottlerocket) purpose-built for Kubernetes production environments.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
GatewayAPI Policy Attachment
Policies add behavior to Gateway API resources, such as authentication, authorization, rate limiting, header manipulation, or security controls.
A policy usually attaches to a target resource (for example a Gateway or a Route) using a targetRef. The exact policy kinds and supported targets depend on the Gateway implementation.
Use policies to separate traffic routing (*Route) from operational and security concerns.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Cross-Namespace Reference Permission (ReferenceGrant)
ReferenceGrant allows a resource in one namespace to reference a resource in another namespace, when the Gateway API would otherwise deny that cross-namespace reference.
It is typically used when a Route in one namespace points to a backend Service in another namespace.
The ReferenceGrant must be created in the target namespace (the namespace of the referenced resource), and it explicitly allows which resource kinds/namespaces may reference it.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
ResourceQuota
ResourceQuota limits the total amount of cluster resources a namespace can consume (for example CPU, memory, storage, and object counts such as pods or services).
From a security and resilience perspective, quotas help reduce denial-of-service risk inside the cluster by preventing a single namespace or team from exhausting shared resources and impacting other workloads.
ResourceQuota is primarily a governance and availability control, but it also supports multi-tenancy and safer operations by enforcing usage bounds.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
LimitRange
LimitRange defines default and minimum/maximum resource requests and limits for containers and pods in a namespace (for example CPU and memory).
From a security and stability perspective, it helps prevent unsafe or unbounded workloads (such as containers with no limits) and improves cluster reliability by enforcing consistent resource settings.
LimitRange is mainly a stability and governance control, but it also supports safer multi-tenant operation by reducing resource abuse and misconfiguration.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Custom Operators / orchestrators
Properly designed custom operators can enhance security by integrating tightly with Kubernetes-native patterns like RBAC, admission control, and CRDs.
For example, you can expose a custom resource that developers use to request infrastructure, while the operator enforces policy-compliant templates and behavior. Operators can also manage resources external to the cluster in a controlled and auditable way.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Exposed port
All containers in a pod share the same network namespace and run on the same node. This allows enforcement of eBPF-based filters and transparent mTLS at the network level.
With sidecars or service mesh integration, unencrypted ports like 80 can safely be exposed internally. Encryption, authentication, and access control are handled outside the application, making this a secure and preferred approach for internal services.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Sidecar container
Sidecar containers can improve security by isolating responsibilities such as TLS termination, authentication, or logging from the main app. They are used by some service meshes (e.g., Istio), but newer approaches like eBPF and ambient meshes offer lower overhead and better scalability.
Sidecars share the same network namespace, allowing secure localhost (127.0.0.1) communication. They can also enforce policies or proxy traffic, but increase attack surface and resource usage.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Init container
Init containers enhance security by performing setup tasks before the main container starts, such as validating configs, downloading secrets, or verifying service dependencies.
They run with separate images and permissions, reducing attack surface in the main container. Types include wait-for-dependency containers, secret fetchers, permission fixers (e.g., chown volumes), and environment validators. Since they run sequentially and exit before app start, they can enforce strict preconditions and avoid persistent exposure.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Ephemeral containers
Ephemeral containers are used for live debugging of running Pods without restarting them. They provide no guarantees on lifecycle, don't support volumes, and can't be part of normal app logic. From a security standpoint, they are powerful but risky—if enabled, they allow runtime inspection, so access should be tightly controlled (e.g., via RBAC).
They share namespaces (like network and PID) with existing containers, enabling deep introspection but also potential abuse if misused.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
WASM containers
WASM containers aim to run WebAssembly modules in place of traditional OCI containers, offering stronger isolation, faster cold starts, and lower resource usage. They don't rely on Linux syscalls, reducing attack surface and making them ideal for sandboxed, untrusted code. Projects like wasmEdge, containerd-shim-wasmedge, and Krustlet explore this in Kubernetes.
Long-term, WASM containers could enable safer multi-tenant workloads and portable compute across cloud, edge, and browser environments.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Hardened container runtimes
Hardened container runtimes provide additional isolation layers beyond standard runtimes like runc. For example, gVisor intercepts syscalls and provides a userspace kernel implementation, while Kata Containers wrap each container in lightweight virtual machines.
OpenShift Sandbox Containers use Kata under the hood to offer enhanced isolation.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
VirtualMachine or other workload-types
Other workload types, such as VirtualMachines (e.g., via KubeVirt), follow the same security mechanisms as pods: RBAC, network policies, storage classes, and admission control.
They are not inherently more privileged and should be treated like any other workload with proper isolation, policy enforcement, and monitoring in place.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Authentication webhook
Authentication webhooks are less commonly used, but can provide additional control beyond standard RBAC. They allow dynamic authentication decisions based on external systems or custom logic.
For example, a webhook can reject requests targeting namespaces that match certain patterns or enforce organization-specific access rules in real time.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Internal API communication
The Kubernetes API should only be accessible to internal system components, operators, and pods that explicitly require it.
Use default-deny NetworkPolicies to block access by default, and only allow specific namespaces or service accounts to communicate with the API server. This minimizes the attack surface and enforces least privilege access.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Cluster to cluster mesh (cluster-mesh)
A cluster-mesh connects multiple Kubernetes clusters to enable cross-cluster communication with cloud-native networking features. This allows services in different clusters to communicate as if they were in the same network.
Traffic can be encrypted using mTLS and authenticated using workload identities unique to each cluster. With proper setup, standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicies can be enforced across cluster boundaries.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
etcd
etcd stores the entire state of the Kubernetes cluster and must be protected accordingly. Enable encryption at rest using the API server's encryption provider configuration.
Access to etcd should be strictly limited to the API server. Ensure mutual TLS is enabled, and never expose etcd directly to the network.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Default ServiceAccount
Every namespace has a default ServiceAccount (unless automountServiceAccountToken=false), and pods use it automatically unless another ServiceAccount is explicitly configured. From a security perspective, this matters because unintended API access can be granted if the default account has permissions or if service account tokens are auto-mounted unnecessarily.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Validating and Mutating Admission Control
Admission controllers intercept API requests after authentication and authorization, allowing for policy enforcement. Tools like Kyverno and OPA Gatekeeper can validate incoming YAML against cluster policies or mutate it to enforce configuration standards (e.g., securityContext, labels, resource limits).
All resources—user-submitted or system-generated—must pass admission control. These controllers can also enforce image signature verification (e.g., cosign) and SLSA provenance checks to prevent untrusted artifacts from being deployed.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
System call filtering (Seccomp)
A pod can restrict which Linux system calls are available to containers using seccomp. This reduces the kernel attack surface by blocking system calls that are not required by the workload.
Kubernetes does not apply system call filtering by default unless seccomp defaulting is enabled on the nodes. A pod can explicitly use the runtime’s default seccomp profile or a custom profile for more restrictive filtering.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 24px; height: 1px; padding-top: 1001px; margin-left: 988px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
Network interfaces (overlay)
Normal kubernetes network is done using an overlay using a CNI (Container Network Interface), like Cilium, Flannel, Calico and many others. They have various functionality and security. Example, some CNIs doesnt support egress network policies, some uses eBPF a lot, some iptables.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
API Priority and Fairness (APF)
API Priority and Fairness controls how incoming API requests are prioritized and rate-limited. Requests are classified into priority levels based on attributes such as the authenticated user, group, or request type.
This protects the API server from overload while ensuring that important requests receive sufficient resources during periods of high demand.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
API to etcd Communication
The Kubernetes API server communicates with etcd to persist cluster state. Read operations (e.g., GET) fetch data directly and do not trigger admission controllers.
Kubernetes also includes the built-in Pod Security Admission (PSA) controller, which enforces the Pod Security Standards (privileged, baseline, restricted) on all created or updated Pods without requiring external webhooks/controllers (it's builtin to the apiserver).
Admission controllers only intercept mutating operations (e.g., CREATE, UPDATE, DELETE). This means read access must be tightly controlled via RBAC/ABAC, since policies cannot be enforced via admission webhooks for those requests.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Mandatory Access Control (MAC)
Mandatory Access Control restricts which resources and operations are available to processes based on security policies enforced by the Linux kernel. This provides an additional security layer beyond traditional Unix permissions and capabilities, limiting what a compromised container can access even when normal permissions would allow it.
In Kubernetes, MAC can be enforced using Linux Security Modules such as AppArmor or SELinux. The available mechanism and its enforcement depend on the operating system and security configuration of the Kubernetes nodes.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 24px; height: 1px; padding-top: 1144px; margin-left: 885px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
AppArmor
A pod can restrict which resources and operations are available to containers using AppArmor. This limits what a compromised process can access, such as files, capabilities, networking, and other kernel-controlled resources.
AppArmor enforcement depends on AppArmor being enabled and supported on the nodes. A pod can explicitly use the runtime’s default AppArmor profile or a custom profile for more restrictive access control.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 19px; height: 1px; padding-top: 1132px; margin-left: 998px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
SELinux
A pod can restrict which resources and operations are available to containers using SELinux. SELinux uses security labels and policies to control how container processes can interact with files, devices, processes, and other system resources.
SELinux enforcement depends on SELinux being enabled and configured on the nodes. A pod can specify SELinux labels through its security context, while the actual access rules are defined by the SELinux policy installed on the node.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 19px; height: 1px; padding-top: 1160px; margin-left: 998px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
Container Runtime Security Policies
A pod can restrict the privileges and runtime environment available to its containers using the Kubernetes security context. These controls can limit container privileges, enforce user and group identities, restrict filesystem access, and reduce access to sensitive kernel functionality.
Runtime security policies can enforce non-root execution, specific user and group IDs, a read-only root filesystem, restricted Linux capabilities, limited /proc access, and prevention of privilege escalation or privileged execution.
These restrictions are configured at the pod or container level and are enforced by Kubernetes, the container runtime, and the underlying Linux kernel.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 24px; height: 1px; padding-top: 1105px; margin-left: 1302px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
Many things in kubernetes can be configured. They are represented this way.
Note that the list of configurables are not complete. Ie, there are often many more capabilities you can configure than those listed.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 17px; height: 1px; padding-top: 962px; margin-left: 197px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
Pod-to-Pod Communication
Each pod has its own cluster IP address and can communicate directly with another pod using that IP.
Because pod IPs are ephemeral, applications normally connect through a Kubernetes Service using its DNS name. DNS resolves the name to the Service’s virtual ClusterIP, which is then translated or routed to one of the backend pod IPs.
Depending on the cluster networking implementation, Service forwarding and load balancing can be handled by kube-proxy using iptables/IPVS, or directly using eBPF.
Pod > Pod IP > Pod
Pod > Service DNS > ClusterIP > Backend Pod
g.data-tags: level-1 info Network Network.Egress Network.Service Network.PodToPod

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 16px; height: 1px; padding-top: 538px; margin-left: 1507px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
Linux Capabilities
Linux capabilities split traditional root privileges into smaller individual permissions that can be granted or removed from containers through the Kubernetes security context.
Common capabilities that can be restricted include NET_ADMIN for network configuration, NET_RAW for raw sockets, SYS_ADMIN for a broad range of administrative operations, SYS_PTRACE for process tracing, SYS_MODULE for kernel module operations, SYS_CHROOT for changing the root directory, MKNOD for creating device nodes, and CHOWN for changing file ownership.
Containers can drop individual capabilities or use drop: ["ALL"] and explicitly add back only the capabilities required by the workload.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Read-Only Root Filesystem
A container can be configured with a read-only root filesystem using the Kubernetes security context.
This prevents processes from modifying the container image filesystem, including application binaries, libraries, and configuration files.
Applications that require writable storage can use explicitly mounted volumes for directories such as temporary files, caches, logs, or persistent application data.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Non-Root Execution
A container can be required to run as a non-root user using the Kubernetes security context.
The runAsNonRoot setting prevents the container from starting if its process would run as UID 0. A specific non-root user and group can also be enforced using runAsUser and runAsGroup.
This prevents workloads from running with root identity inside the container and reduces the privileges available to the application process.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 122, 122), rgb(198, 84, 84)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(184, 84, 80), rgb(215, 129, 126));

g.data-help:
Volume definitions
Pods can use different volume types, some of which may expose sensitive host resources to containers.
Volume types such as hostPath can provide direct access to the node filesystem and are commonly restricted in security-sensitive environments. Workloads should only be allowed to use volume types required for their operation.
Admission policies can restrict or deny unsafe volume types and validate how volumes are configured before a pod is created.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Kubelet and API Server Communication
The kubelet is the Kubernetes agent running on each worker node and communicates directly with the Kubernetes API server.
The kubelet acts as a client of the Kubernetes API, registering the node, reporting node and pod status, and watching for pods assigned to its node. Changes are received through API watches, allowing the kubelet to continuously reconcile the desired state with the containers running on the node.
The API server can also connect to the Kubelet API, typically on port 10250, for operations such as container logs, exec, and attach.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 15px; height: 1px; padding-top: 76px; margin-left: 972px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 9px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
Kubelet API Access and NodeRestriction
Kubelets authenticate to the Kubernetes API using their node identity and should only be permitted to access resources required for their own node.
The Node authorizer limits what authenticated kubelets can access, while the NodeRestriction admission plugin further restricts which Node and Pod objects a kubelet is allowed to modify.
Together, these controls help prevent a compromised kubelet from modifying other nodes, changing pods assigned to other nodes, or manipulating protected node labels that could influence workload scheduling.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
OCI Container
A container is not a virtual machine, but an isolated Linux process running directly on the worker node’s kernel.
The container runtime creates the process according to the OCI specification and configures its filesystem, namespaces, cgroups, capabilities, security controls, environment, and other runtime settings.
Kubernetes typically uses a CRI runtime such as containerd or CRI-O, which in turn uses an OCI runtime such as runc or crun to create and start the container process.
After startup, the workload runs as normal Linux processes isolated and restricted by kernel mechanisms.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 24px; height: 1px; padding-top: 917px; margin-left: 863px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
Scheduler & Controller Manager > API Server
The kube-scheduler and kube-controller-manager act as clients of the Kubernetes API and initiate authenticated HTTPS connections to the API server.
Both use list/watch requests to continuously observe cluster state and write changes back through the API. The scheduler assigns pods to nodes, while the controller-manager reconciles resources toward their desired state.
All requests are authenticated and authorized by the API server. Neither component accesses etcd directly.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 15px; height: 1px; padding-top: 113px; margin-left: 762px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 9px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
The kube-controller-manager runs the core controllers responsible for continuously reconciling the desired state stored in Kubernetes with the observed state of the cluster.
It contains multiple independent control loops, including controllers for Nodes, ReplicaSets, Deployments, Jobs, Namespaces, ServiceAccounts, and many other Kubernetes resources.
Controllers continuously list and watch resources through the Kubernetes API.
When the observed state differs from the desired state, they create, update, or delete resources through the API to move the cluster toward the desired state. They do not communicate directly with the scheduler, kubelet, or etcd.
The controller-manager operates using its own authenticated identity and requires broad cluster-wide API permissions because its controllers manage many different resource types.
From a security perspective, the controller-manager is one of the most privileged control-plane components. Compromise of its identity or credentials can provide extensive control over cluster resources, making protection of its credentials, configuration, and host particularly important.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 15px; height: 1px; padding-top: 123px; margin-left: 652px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 9px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
Kube-Scheduler
The kube-scheduler is responsible for selecting which node should run each newly created Pod that has not yet been assigned to a node.
It continuously watches the Kubernetes API for unscheduled Pods and maintains information about Nodes and other resources required to make scheduling decisions. It considers available resources, scheduling constraints, affinity, taints and tolerations, topology, and other scheduling policies.
Once a node has been selected, the scheduler records the decision through the Kubernetes API. It does not communicate directly with the kubelet or etcd.
The scheduler operates using its own authenticated identity and requires cluster-wide read access to several resources, while its write permissions are primarily related to scheduling Pods. Its API access is controlled through Kubernetes authorization, typically RBAC.
From a security perspective, the scheduler is highly trusted because it can influence where workloads execute. However, its API privileges are generally more limited than those of the kube-controller-manager.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 15px; height: 1px; padding-top: 122px; margin-left: 623px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 9px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
Kubernetes Resources
Kubernetes resources are API objects that describe the desired or observed state of the cluster. Examples include Pods, Deployments, Services, Secrets, Nodes, Roles, and NetworkPolicies.
Resources can be created by users and applications through the Kubernetes API, or automatically by controllers and other Kubernetes components. Controllers continuously watch resources and may create, modify, or delete other resources to reconcile the cluster toward its desired state.
Namespaced resources belong to a specific namespace and are commonly used for workloads and their configuration. Examples include Pods, Deployments, Services, Secrets, ConfigMaps, and Roles.
Cluster-scoped resources exist across the entire cluster and do not belong to a namespace. Examples include Nodes, Namespaces, ClusterRoles, StorageClasses, and PersistentVolumes.
All resources are accessed and managed through the Kubernetes API, where authentication, authorization, admission control, and other security controls determine who can perform operations on them.

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 17px; height: 1px; padding-top: 918px; margin-left: 197px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
Cloud-Native Application Protection Platform (CNAPP)
A CNAPP provides centralized security visibility and protection across Kubernetes, containers, cloud infrastructure, and workloads.
It typically combines vulnerability and image scanning, security posture management, identity and permission analysis, compliance monitoring, and runtime threat detection.
A CNAPP helps identify and prioritize risks across multiple security layers instead of evaluating vulnerabilities and misconfigurations in isolation.
Examples: Wiz, Sysdig, Prisma Cloud, and Aqua Security.
Open-source building blocks: Kubescape, Trivy, Falco and NeuVector, some of them for just scanning images for vulnerabilities in a remote repository.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
NodePort
A NodePort exposes a Service on a static port on every Kubernetes node.
Traffic sent to <NodeIP>:<NodePort> is forwarded by the Kubernetes networking implementation to one of the Service's backend Pods.
NodePort provides basic external reachability, but does not itself provision an external load balancer or public IP.
g.data-tags: level-3 info Network Network.Ingress Ingress Ingress.Controller

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 16px; height: 1px; padding-top: 118px; margin-left: 1680px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 9px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
LoadBalancer
A LoadBalancer Service requests an external load balancer from an integrated cloud provider or load-balancer implementation such as MetalLB.
The load balancer receives an external IP and forwards traffic into the Kubernetes Service, which then distributes traffic to its backend Pods.
A LoadBalancer Service typically builds on the same Service mechanisms as NodePort, although implementations may route traffic differently and can bypass NodePort.
g.data-tags: level-3 info Network Network.Ingress Ingress Ingress.GatewayApi Ingress.GatewayApi.Gateway

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 16px; height: 1px; padding-top: 138px; margin-left: 1680px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 9px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
NodePort Exposure
By default, Kubernetes reserves ports 30000-32767 for NodePort Services. A NodePort is normally exposed on eligible network interfaces of every node, meaning <NodeIP>:<NodePort> can provide an entry point to the Service.
The port range can be changed using the kube-apiserver option: --service-node-port-range=30000-32767
Which node addresses accept NodePort traffic can be restricted using the kube-proxy --nodeport-addresses option. This allows NodePort to bind only to selected node networks, for example an internal network.
Network firewalls should additionally restrict access to the NodePort range from untrusted networks.
Note: CNI implementations such as Cilium may implement NodePort without kube-proxy and provide their own configuration for controlling exposure.
g.data-tags: level-3 info Network Network.Ingress Ingress Ingress.Controller

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 8px; height: 1px; padding-top: 175px; margin-left: 1746px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 9px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
Load Balancer in Front of NodePort
A load balancer provides a controlled external entry point and forwards traffic to the NodePort on selected Kubernetes nodes.
It provides a stable IP or hostname, distributes traffic between healthy nodes, and prevents clients from needing direct access to individual nodes.
Firewall rules should restrict NodePort access so that only the load balancer can reach the exposed ports.
g.data-tags: level-3 info Network Network.Ingress Ingress Ingress.Controller

rect.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(223, 244, 255), rgb(15, 33, 42)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(11, 111, 164), rgb(86, 172, 218));

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe center; width: 12px; height: 1px; padding-top: 168px; margin-left: 1774px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: center; color: #0A3D5A;
display: inline-block; font-size: 9px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#0A3D5A, #9cc8e1); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

g.data-help:
Signed Git Commits
Git commits should be signed using a hardware security key (e.g., YubiKey) to ensure authenticity. ArgoCD can be configured to verify commit signatures before deployment.
g.data-tags: level-2 pri-2 SupplyChain SupplyChain.Git SupplyChain.Gitops SupplyChain.Signing

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
git (application)
The git-forge (example gitlab, forgejo, ..), that the service-owner/developer uses can be hosted inside the same cluster. A good pattern is to keep this separate from the platform-git.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Argocd (service owner)
To keep the argocd that deals with platform and infrastructure separate from application is good practice. The argocd that deploy the developer applications shoulnt have access to the service-accounts that handles cluster-wide and important resources.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Argocd (operator)
The argocd used by the platform team should be running on a separate cluster. It contains credentials with admin privileges to the cluster it manages. Thats why we run it outside the cluster, so nothing inside the cluster can access it.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Git operator 2
For git operations that can have big impact, there should be "4-eyes" before the change is live. This can be done with protected branches, but also signing of the git-repo itself using tools like gittuf.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Image Builder
The image builder produces trusted artifacts and must maintain verifiable build provenance. Each image should be linked to its source commit, build identity, SBOM, and resulting image digest.
Build provenance and attestations should be signed and stored in an append-only transparency log, such as Sigstore Rekor, allowing the origin and integrity of deployed images to be independently verified.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
User Namespace
Linux user namespaces isolate user and group identities between a container and the host.
UIDs and GIDs inside the namespace can be mapped to different IDs outside it. This allows UID 0 (root) inside a container to be mapped to an unprivileged UID on the host.
In Kubernetes, this isolation can be enabled for a pod using hostUsers: false, which automatically assigns and manages the UID/GID mapping.
This provides an additional isolation boundary and limits the privileges of container processes on the host.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 122, 122), rgb(198, 84, 84)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(184, 84, 80), rgb(215, 129, 126));

g.data-help:
Virtual Machine Resources
The resources visible to the guest are virtual hardware provided by QEMU/KVM and configured through the VirtualMachine specification.
vCPUs are backed by QEMU execution threads scheduled on host CPUs, while virtual memory is backed by memory allocated to the virt-launcher pod. Virtual disks are typically backed by PVCs or DataVolumes, and virtual NICs are connected through the pod's networking or additional network attachments.
KubeVirt translates the VM configuration into the required pod resources, devices and runtime configuration. Kubernetes cgroups and resource limits therefore still control the underlying host resources available to the VM.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Other cluster nodes
Inter-node traffic may use direct IP-to-IP communication or be encapsulated, depending on the CNI configuration. Encryption can be applied at this level via service mesh (e.g., mTLS) or CNI-level encryption.
Certain workloads—such as ingress controllers, operators, or AI/ML jobs—should be scheduled on dedicated nodes using taints, tolerations, or node selectors to enforce separation and reduce security risk.
There can be many different types of nodes.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
SBOM
A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) provides a machine-readable inventory of the components and dependencies contained in an image.
It enables continuous vulnerability assessment, license tracking, and rapid identification of affected workloads when new vulnerabilities are discovered.
SBOMs should be generated during the build, associated with the image digest, and stored alongside the artifact using standards such as SPDX or CycloneDX.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Provenance / Attestation
Provenance describes where an artifact came from and how it was produced, while attestations provide verifiable claims about the artifact and its build process.
Attestations can link an image digest to its source commit, build system, dependencies, SBOM, and security checks, creating a verifiable chain from source to deployment.
They should be cryptographically signed and verified before deployment, ensuring that only artifacts produced through trusted build processes are allowed to run.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Secure CNI (e.g., Cilium)
Use a CNI plugin that supports fine-grained network policies and visibility, such as Cilium with eBPF. Define a baseline deny-all policy and explicitly allow only required traffic.
Default Kubernetes network policies are namespace-scoped and may not cover all scenarios.
g.data-tags: level-3 pri-2 Node Node.Observability Network Network.Cni Node.Observability.Datapath

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Network Observability (e.g., Hubble)
Deploy network observability tooling that provides workload-aware visibility into network flows, policy verdicts, and DNS activity.
Retain flow telemetry centrally to enable historical correlation between network indicators and Kubernetes workloads during incident investigation.
Network observability complements network policy enforcement but does not replace it.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Runtime Security and Observability (e.g., Tetragon, Falco)
Use runtime security tooling to observe process execution, system calls, network connections, and other security-relevant activity inside workloads.
Correlate runtime events with Kubernetes metadata to identify which process, container, and workload caused suspicious activity.
Runtime visibility provides context that network telemetry alone cannot provide.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Runtime Security (e.g., Tetragon)
Use eBPF-based runtime security to observe and control process execution, network activity, and other kernel-level behavior with Kubernetes workload context.
Tracing policies can provide targeted visibility and enforcement for security-sensitive runtime activity.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Runtime Threat Detection (e.g., Falco)
Use runtime threat detection to identify suspicious behavior such as unexpected process execution, privilege changes, sensitive file access, and unusual network activity.
Tune detection rules to the expected behavior of workloads and forward alerts to a central security monitoring system.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Node-Level Security
Some security controls operate at the Kubernetes node and Linux kernel level rather than inside individual pods or containers.
Node-level controls can provide visibility and enforcement across workloads, including network datapaths, process execution, system calls, and other kernel-observable activity.

g.data-help:
Security Logging and Monitoring
Kubernetes security-relevant logs should be collected centrally and forwarded to a remote logging or SIEM platform such as Splunk for monitoring, correlation, alerting, and long-term retention.
Important sources include Kubernetes API audit logs, control-plane component logs, kubelet and container runtime logs, authentication and authorization events, admission controller decisions, CNI/network security logs, and security events generated by runtime detection tools.
Kubernetes Audit Logging is particularly important because it records requests made to the Kubernetes API, including who performed an action, which resource was accessed or modified, and whether the request was allowed or denied.
Logs should be stored outside the cluster or otherwise protected from workloads and compromised nodes to prevent attackers from modifying or deleting security evidence.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Multi-interface (Multus)
A pod can have multiple network interfaces using the Multus CNI plugin. This allows attaching additional networks to a pod beyond the default CNI.
It is useful for scenarios like separating control and data planes, connecting to legacy networks, or assigning dedicated interfaces for specific protocols.

g.data-help:
Network interfaces (underlay)
Pods can use different types of network interfaces depending on requirements. Containers can bind directly to the host interface, or use other means to communicate over vlans and such.
Be aware: underlay networks (e.g., macvlan) typically bypass Kubernetes NetworkPolicies. Overlay networks used by most CNIs enforce policy as expected and are safer by default.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Host Networking
hostNetwork is technically neither overlay nor underlay networking. The pod shares the node’s network namespace and uses the node’s interfaces and IP addresses directly instead of receiving a normal pod network namespace.
This reduces network isolation, may bypass normal pod-level NetworkPolicy enforcement depending on the CNI, and can expose node-local services, interfaces, and ports to the workload.
Host networking should therefore normally be restricted and only allowed when explicitly required.
It goes mostly in/out the same way as underlay.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
NetworkPolicy Enforcement
NetworkPolicies are applied to pods, not Kubernetes Services. A policy selects pods using labels and controls the ingress and/or egress traffic allowed for those pods.
Enforcement happens on the pod network path and ultimately applies to traffic between pod IPs. This means the same policy applies whether traffic reaches a pod through a Service or connects directly to the pod IP.
Services may select the same pods for routing and load balancing, but they are not the enforcement point for NetworkPolicies.

g.data-help:
Egress
Egress policies control outbound traffic from pods using label selectors and destination IPs or CIDRs. These rules help prevent unauthorized external access.
Some CNIs support assigning dedicated egress IPs per namespace or pod, enabling traceability and firewall integration for outbound traffic control.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));

g.data-help:
Traffic before filters
Traffic before reaching L7 filters (e.g., Envoy) is often encrypted with mTLS. This makes payload inspection impossible, but metadata such as SNI, client identity, or source IP can still be used to enforce context-aware ACLs.
Use this metadata to apply fine-grained policies even when the content is opaque.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 209, 161), rgb(85, 46, 4)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(180, 95, 6), rgb(208, 135, 58));

g.data-help:
Traffic after filters
This is the raw, decrypted traffic that reaches the application after passing through L7 filters or service mesh proxies. At this point, the traffic is no longer encrypted and can be inspected or modified by sidecars or host-level tools before delivery to the application process.
Ensure that applications enforce their own validation and security controls, as traffic is now trusted and inside the protected boundary.

ellipse.style: fill: light-dark(rgb(255, 242, 166), rgb(45, 34, 0)); stroke: light-dark(rgb(182, 138, 0), rgb(156, 119, 0));
